core_principles.text: An upright trunk tends to create a 90/90 lunge where both knees are at 90-degree angles at the bottom of the movement.
A slight forward lean of the trunk positions the upper body weight over the mid-thigh, distributing demand evenly across the hip, knee, and ankle.
To increase gluteus maximus involvement, add trunk rotation toward the forward leg combined with a slight forward trunk lean.
Keep the forward heel on the ground and distribute weight evenly across the forward foot to maximize glute involvement.
Maintain solid hip, knee, and ankle alignment during multiplanar lunges.
Avoid taking strides that are too long to ensure control is maintained throughout the entire range of motion.
Reach toward the ground with your hands as you step to soften the landing and reinforce eccentric control.

common_mistakes.text: Lifting the forward heel off the ground while decelerating toward the floor.
Taking strides that are too long, which leads to using momentum to propel oneself back up.

specific_findings.text: An upright trunk tends to create what is often called a 90/90 lunge where both knees at the bottom of the move are 90° angles.
To increase gluteus maximus involvement, rotate the right shoulder toward the left knee when performing a lunge with the left foot forward.
Use a client's reach to guide them into different planes by having them reach for 12:00 or 9:00 as if standing in the center of an imaginary clock.

consequences.text: In an upright lunge, the forward knee experiences more torque because it is the joint farthest from the load of the body, forcing the knee extensors to bear more responsibility.
Taking strides that are too long causes the exerciser to use momentum to propel themselves up, which reduces control throughout the range of motion.

core_principles.text: Stand with the feet hip-width apart and grip one dumbbell in each hand with the palms facing each other and the arms straight down by the side.
Keep the back straight when stepping forward.
As the front foot hits the floor, lower the back knee towards the floor.
Descend to a comfortable range of motion and push the front foot into the ground to stand up by bringing both feet back together at the starting position.
Have space between your legs to help with balance.
The length of the lunge should be about two times your hip width.
Keep the front foot always on the ground, with the whole foot rooted on the floor.
Keep your body straight at all times, avoiding leaning forward or backward when standing or stepping.
Ensure the front knee stays behind the toes during the lunge.

common_mistakes.text: Making the lunge step too short or too long.
Placing feet on the same line, which reduces stability.
Allowing the front knee to collapse inward.
Having a shaky front knee during the movement.
Allowing the front foot to be unstable on the ground.
Leaning the torso forward or backward.
Performing jerky movements, particularly when stepping back.
Keeping the back knee too low when the leg lacks the necessary strength.
Pushing aggressively against the ground, particularly when stepping back.
Allowing the front heel to come off the ground.
Allowing the knees to go over the toes.
Maintaining poor posture during the exercise.

consequences.text: Incorrect lunge technique can lead to knee pain.
Incorrect lunge technique can lead to ankle pain.
Incorrect lunge technique can lead to foot pain.
Incorrect lunge technique can lead to back pain.
Incorrect lunge technique can lead to shoulder pain.
Incorrect lunge technique can promote poor posture.
Incorrect lunge technique can result in not training the right muscles and straining others.
If the lunge step is too short, the front heel may come off the ground.
If the lunge step is too long, you may have to lean forward to step.
